podcast.title: Attempted Murder-for-Hire (May 7, 2023)
podcast.body: Tim Lambesis, frontman of the San Diego metalcore band, hired what he believed was a hitman to kill his estranged wife, Megan, reportedly due to a dispute over his desire to focus on record producing versus her wanting him to tour for income. Lambesis offered $20,000 for the act. "The story is that he hired a hitman to kill Megan, his estranged wife."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Most Dangerous Artists in Rock

podcast.title: Arrest and Conviction
podcast.body: The "hitman" Lambesis hired turned out to be an undercover police officer, leading to his arrest on May 7, 2023. He was subsequently tried and convicted before any harm could come to Megan. "But then the hitman he hired turned out to be an undercover cop."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Most Dangerous Artists in Rock

podcast.title: Attempted Murder-for-Hire Plot
podcast.body: On May 7, 2013, Tim Lambesis was arrested in Oceanside, California, charged with attempting to hire a hitman to kill his wife. The plot originated when he discussed killing his wife with his steroid dealer at the gym, who then reported him to the police. Law enforcement set up a sting operation, where Lambesis met with an undercover detective. "On May 7, 2013, Lombicis was arrested in the Ocean Side, California. He was charged with trying to hire a hitman to kill the woman he wanted to divorce."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Christian Identity and Philanthropy
podcast.body: As I Lay Dying, a band from San Diego, created music with pro-Christian themes for years, with all members, including singer Tim Lambesis, professing strong Christian beliefs. While their lyrics didn't explicitly mention God or Jesus, their spiritual stance was clear, and Tim even appeared on Christian radio shows. Tim seemed to be a family man, having adopted three children from Ethiopia with his wife. "They've never really been explicit about it. There's no direct mentions of God or Jesus or anything like that in their lyrics, but they've made it very clear where they stand spiritually."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Guilty Plea and Prison Sentence
podcast.body: Initially, Tim Lambesis pleaded not guilty to the charges, with his lawyers arguing that excessive steroid use had impaired his judgment. However, on February 25, 2014, he changed his plea to guilty. On May 14, he was sentenced to six years in prison for his role in the murder-for-hire plot. "But then on February 25, 2014, he changed his plea to guilty. On May 14, he was sentenced to six years in prison."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Incarceration and Band Reformation
podcast.body: Lambesis was sentenced to six years in prison. While he was incarcerated, As I Lay Dying continued under a different name with another vocalist. Upon his release on probation in December 2016, the original group reformed and has since been touring and recording. "He was sentenced to six years in prison."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Most Dangerous Artists in Rock

podcast.title: Loss of Faith and Divorce
podcast.body: In the summer of 2012, Tim Lambesis began to struggle with the tenets of organized religion. He communicated to his wife via letter that he no longer believed in God and wished for a divorce. Concurrently, he became heavily involved in bodybuilding and started seeing other women, which was contrary to his professed Christian values. His wife, understandably upset, reportedly made threats about cutting him off from their adopted children. "In the summer of 2012, he began to struggle with the tenets of organized religion. Tim wrote home to his wife. I no longer believe in God. Oh, and I wanted a divorce."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Post-Conviction Consequences
podcast.body: Following his sentencing, Tim Lambesis faced severe financial and personal repercussions. His ex-wife filed a $2 million civil suit against him and was granted a 10-year restraining order. All family assets, amounting to hundreds of thousands of dollars, were turned over to his ex-wife. Furthermore, Tim's parents agreed to relinquish all grandparent rights to the three adopted children from Ethiopia. "His ex-wife filed a $2 million civil suit against him. He also has a 10-year restraining order."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Professed Christianity
podcast.body: Despite the attempted murder-for-hire, all members of As I Lay Dying, including Tim Lambesis, publicly profess to be practicing Christians. "All the members in As I Lay Dying, including Lembesis, profess to be practicing Christians."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Most Dangerous Artists in Rock

podcast.title: Remorse and Allegations of Setup
podcast.body: Tim Lambesis is described as very clear-headed and remorseful about the entire situation, acknowledging the stupidity of his actions. However, deeper investigation into the case suggests why he might feel he was set up, hinting at complexities beyond his initial actions. "Anacasia wondering, Tim is very clear-headed and very remorseful about the whole thing. He knows it was stupid, but if you dig into the case more, you can see why he feels he was set up."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Sting Operation and Arrest Details
podcast.body: During the sting operation, Tim Lambesis met with an undercover detective. He provided the detective with a thousand dollars in cash, photographs of his wife, her home address, and the alarm codes for her house. He was arrested immediately after handing over the envelope in the parking lot of a Barnes and Noble bookstore. "As soon as he handed over the envelope in the parking lot of a Barnes and Noble bookstore, he was arrested."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
